findings.text: The first sentence says plainly what Athena is, so a newcomer knows right away what the site is about.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository.

findings.text: The header explains why the page exists and why it matters: it shows Athena working, and every statement can be checked. The claim ids link to source lines at a pinned commit, which backs this up.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: The header links to a next step, so a newcomer doesn't have to scroll past the long firstmate material to find what to do.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself

findings.text: This is Athena's site address, but the title and almost all of the page are about firstmate, a different project. Athena gets two sentences. A newcomer may wonder whether this is Athena's homepage or a side example, and learns little about how Athena itself is used.
The header says Athena checks work with a second model and records costs. Nothing on the page shows either one, so a newcomer has to take these selling points on faith.
findings.source: has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost

findings.text: The install step assumes you already have a checkout. It gives no clone command and no prerequisites (for example a Rust toolchain or model API keys), so a newcomer would have to leave the page to find out how to get started.
findings.source: Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh

findings.text: The walkthrough uses words like "place", "spawn", "teardown" and "exit 75" before defining them. They aren't in the "Words used first" list, and their definitions are only in the Glossary further down.
findings.source: One piece of work, start to finish

findings.text: The rules for yolo, red and in-scope work are repeated almost word for word in the definitions, the overview, the walkthrough, the failure list, the t4 and t10 cards, and the Glossary. This makes an already dense page longer and harder for a newcomer to skim.
The page is honest that it doesn't know what "in scope" means. That still leaves a gap in the core explanation of how merging works.
findings.source: in scope ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it.

findings.text: This section only names an internal folder ("studies/"), which means nothing to someone who hasn't installed Athena.
